findings.claim: The public key is only checked for presence at boot via getOrThrow, so a malformed or truncated PEM (common with env-var newline mangling) will pass startup and then cause every webhook verification to fail. The module claims to fail fast at boot, but that guarantee is not actually enforced; the constructor or config validator should attempt crypto.createPublicKey to validate the PEM at startup.

The Authorization header is typed as string | string[] | undefined, but the code calls header?.startsWith('Bearer ') without checking the type; if the header is ever an array, this throws and results in an uncaught 500 error instead of the intended UnauthorizedException.

expiresInDays has no upper bound, so a typo such as --expires-in 18250 would mint a token valid for roughly 50 years, far outliving the key rotation lifecycle; an upper cap (e.g. 10 years) should be enforced and a warning logged when the resolved value exceeds some threshold.

Because iss equals aud by design, any other CGW-minted token targeted at itself for a different purpose would satisfy the iss and aud checks; the actual protection against crossover comes from a separate layer (SERVICE_ACCESS role/markers), and this dependency should be made explicit with an inline comment on verify().

The main() function handles two signing modes (KMS and local) in a single ~60-line function; it should be split into separate mintViaKms and mintLocally functions, leaving main to handle argument parsing, orchestration, and printing.

KmsSignerConfig, IKmsSigner, and resolveCredentials are defined across two files instead of being consolidated; they should be moved into a dedicated interface/types file so the service file contains only the implementation.

BillingAuthService mixes DI-instance responsibilities (verify) with static factory methods (mint, mintViaSigner) that have no relation to the injected service other than sharing buildClaims; extracting a separate BillingTokenMinter module used by the CLI would remove the CLI's dependency on the DI-decorated class and make the 'app never signs' boundary structural rather than conventional.
Constants and the BillingTokenClaimsArgs type are defined in billing-auth.service.ts but belong next to the entity/schema for consistency with the rest of the module.

The test suite never asserts the webIdentityTokenFile branch of resolveCredentials, leaving the IRSA credential path untested; a test case constructing with { webIdentityTokenFile: '...' } should be added.

There is a coverage gap where the guard integration tests do not cover a token whose aud is an array containing the expected issuer alongside other values; since verify accepts a string audience against an array, a regression here could silently loosen authentication, so a test signing a token with aud: [ISSUER, 'other'] expecting a 202 response should be added.

The BillingServiceTokenSchema spec uses literal strings ('SERVICE_ACCESS', 'SERVICE_USER') instead of importing the exported constants (e.g. SERVICE_ACCESS_ROLE), creating a small risk of drift if the constant values change.

Using path: '' together with @Post('/billing/webhooks') is awkward; giving the controller path: 'billing' and the route 'webhooks' would read more naturally and match the rest of the codebase's conventions.

The AUTH_HEADER_NAME constant declared inside BillingWebhookAuthGuard.getBearerToken has no reuse value as a local constant; it should either be lifted to a module-level constant or the indirection should be dropped.
SignCommand accepts a Uint8Array, making the Buffer.from(response.Signature) call on line 51 an unnecessary no-op copy since Buffer is already a Uint8Array on Node; the same applies to getPublicKey.
